intro_band.agent_remit_summary: The remit governs `deepagents-cli`, a deterministic developer command-line tool that scaffolds, validates, bundles, and deploys a Managed Deep Agents project to the LangSmith platform and manages the workspace agents and MCP servers it references. It performs no LLM inference itself — it assembles the agent payload and managed-directory tree only from the project's declared sources (`agent.json`, `AGENTS.md`, `tools.json`, `skills/`, `subagents/`) and upserts over HTTPS with the developer's own `LANGSMITH_API_KEY`. Its authorized counterparties are the platform API and Hub at `api.smith.langchain.com`, the local terminal, and the project directory and `~/.deepagents/`; it must never fold credentials into the bundle, follow symlinks or path-escapes out of the project root, deploy over non-HTTPS or non-TLS endpoints, auto-register MCP servers, or update a remote agent declared by `agent_id` without confirmation.
intro_band.agent_structure_summary: A Python 3.11+ CLI (`deepagents-cli` v0.2.2, MIT) whose shipped surface is `deepagents_cli/` under `libs/cli/`, wiring four argparse subcommands — `init`, `deploy`, `agents`, `mcp-servers` — in `main.py`; a bare `deepagents` invocation prints a redirect to the separate `deepagents-code` REPL and exits non-zero. Deploy logic lives in `deploy/`: `project.py` parses and containment-checks the project (rejecting symlinks and path-escapes), `payload.py` builds the bundle as a pure function over the parsed project, `mcp_resolver.py` validates referenced MCP servers against the live workspace, `api_client.py` is an `httpx` client (`trust_env=False`) that forces HTTPS and rejects userinfo, and `state.py` keeps last-deploy metadata under `~/.deepagents/`. There is no model client, exec, or subprocess in the deploy surface; the only outbound traffic is to the platform host plus a browser launch for MCP OAuth. A `THREAT_MODEL.md` ships but predates the REPL split and describes surfaces no longer in this package.

behavior_summary: This is a mature, security-conscious deterministic CLI whose declared boundaries are largely enforced in code: HTTPS-with-no-userinfo transport (`api_client._normalize_endpoint`, `trust_env=False`), project-`.env` blocking of endpoint/proxy/TLS overrides, symlink and path-escape rejection during bundle assembly (`project._ensure_project_contained`), confirmation gates on remote-mutating and destructive actions, and MCP auth-header redaction. The dominant pattern is *declared-transport-security enforced for the platform endpoint but not re-applied to referenced MCP-server URLs*: neither `mcp-servers add` nor `deploy` validates that a remote MCP URL uses TLS, so the remit's "MUST use TLS" rule for MCP servers is unenforced (and, tellingly, untested) while the analogous platform-endpoint rule is both enforced and tested. The remaining findings are posture gaps rather than exploitable chains — two dependencies lack upper version bounds, the shipped threat model no longer matches the shipped code, and the documented `--header X-Api-Key=$SECRET` workflow places credentials on the command line.

rules.rule_text: Assemble the agent payload and managed-directory file tree **only** from the project's declared sources, then upsert the agent on `/v1/deepagents/agents` (create when new, patch metadata + commit Hub directory when it already exists).
Parse and validate a project directory into a structured payload (`deepagents deploy`), rejecting malformed configuration before anything is shipped.
Validate that every MCP server URL referenced by the project is already registered in the workspace and invocable by the caller's identity — never auto-registering servers during deploy.
Offer a `--dry-run` that prints the exact payload and directory files it would send, without contacting any mutating endpoint.
Running the deployed agent itself, or performing any LLM inference — the CLI produces the artifact and hands it to the platform; it never invokes a model.
Acting as an interactive coding assistant or REPL — that surface moved to the separate `deepagents-code` (`dcode`) package; a bare `deepagents` invocation only redirects the user there.
Sending email, posting to social/external services, or making outbound calls beyond the deployment platform and its Hub / tracing services.
Default endpoint `https://api.smith.langchain.com`; scheme forced to HTTPS, userinfo rejected, proxy env ignored (`trust_env=False`).
Letting repository-local deploy state steer authenticated requests (auth resolution ignores repo-local state).
Writing, committing to version control, logging, or printing platform / provider / Hub / tracing credentials or MCP auth-header values.
Folding secret material (e.g. `.env` contents) into the seeded bundle payload — environment stays environment; it is never merged into the skills, subagent, or managed-directory payload.
Pulling any file into the bundle from outside the resolved project root, via symlink, path traversal, or an undeclared source.

Deploying to an `agent_id` declared in `agent.json` that local state has not previously confirmed — the CLI must show the target agent name/id and require a `y/N` confirmation before updating that remote agent (bypassable only with `--yes`).
Overwriting an existing project folder during `init` (requires `--force`).
Deleting a workspace agent or MCP server (requires `y/N` confirmation or `--yes`).
Reaching the platform over a non-HTTPS endpoint, or one carrying userinfo.
Bundling, registering, or deploying a project that references a remote MCP server over a non-TLS URL (`http://` / `ws://`) — remote MCP server URLs MUST use TLS (`https` / `wss`).
Auto-registering an MCP server, or deploying while a referenced MCP server is unregistered or uninvocable by the caller's identity.
Creating a fresh agent via `--reset` while `agent.json` still declares an `agent_id`.
A project input is a symlink or escapes the project root — stop.
The resolved endpoint is not HTTPS or carries userinfo, or `LANGSMITH_API_KEY` is missing — stop before any request.
Each invocation runs to completion and exits; it does not linger or poll except for the bounded post-deploy health check and OAuth session polling (with a `--timeout`).
Subcommands `init`, `deploy`, `agents`, `mcp-servers` — and nothing that invokes a model, opens a REPL, or spawns a local server.
Dependencies are expected to be version-controlled with a committed, pinned lockfile.

findings.summary: Neither `mcp-servers add` nor `deploy` validates that a referenced remote MCP server URL uses TLS, so `http://`/`ws://` servers are registered and deployed unchecked.
findings.description: The remit forbids registering or deploying a project that references a non-TLS MCP URL, requiring `https`/`wss`. `_execute_mcp_server_add` passes `args.url` straight to `create_mcp_server` with no scheme check, and `resolve_referenced_servers` only lowercases and trailing-slash-strips URLs (`_normalize_url`) while confirming registration and invocability — never the scheme. The platform-endpoint TLS rule is enforced and tested, but the MCP-URL rule is neither; scored High rather than Critical because the plaintext hop is downstream of the CLI (platform/agent runtime) and requires the developer to supply an http URL.
policy_rule_text: Bundling, registering, or deploying a project that references a remote MCP server over a non-TLS URL (`http://` / `ws://`) — remote MCP server URLs MUST use TLS (`https` / `wss`).

evidence.snippet: _execute_mcp_server_add passes args.url to client.create_mcp_server with no https/wss scheme validation
_normalize_url lowercases and strips trailing slash only; resolve_referenced_servers checks registration/invocability but never the URL scheme

recommended_actions: In `commands._execute_mcp_server_add` (and `_execute_mcp_server_update`), reject any `--url` whose scheme is not `https`/`wss` before calling `create_mcp_server`.

In `mcp_resolver.resolve_referenced_servers` (or `project._read_tools_json`), fail the deploy when any referenced `mcp_server_url` is not TLS, so a previously-registered non-TLS server cannot ride through.

findings.summary: Two runtime dependencies are floor-pinned with no upper bound, so a PyPI install can resolve an unvetted future major version despite the committed lockfile.
findings.description: `pyproject.toml` caps most dependencies with an upper bound (`langchain>=1.3.12,<2.0.0`, `httpx>=0.28.1,<1.0.0`) but leaves `deepagents>=0.6.12` and `langsmith>=0.9.3` open-ended. The committed `uv.lock` protects reproducible in-repo installs, but `uv tool install deepagents-cli` from PyPI resolves the ranges fresh and could pull a breaking or compromised major version of either package. This is posture, not an active exploit — add ceilings to match the rest of the dependency set.

evidence.snippet: "deepagents>=0.6.12" and "langsmith>=0.9.3" have no upper bound while peer deps carry <2.0.0 / <1.0.0 caps

recommended_actions: Add upper bounds to the `deepagents` and `langsmith` requirements in `libs/cli/pyproject.toml` (e.g. `<1.0.0`) consistent with the other pinned dependencies.

findings.summary: The shipped threat model predates the REPL split and documents surfaces the package no longer contains, leaving the current deploy surface unmodeled.
findings.description: `THREAT_MODEL.md` carries a top-of-file warning that it was generated before the 0.1.0 split and that its TUI, MCP, sandbox, sessions, server-subprocess, hooks, and skills sections no longer apply — yet its entire body (components C1–C17, threats T1–T10) still describes the retired REPL, including surfaces like the unauthenticated `langgraph dev` server and `class_path` code execution that are absent from `deepagents_cli/deploy`. The current bundler, MCP resolver, and credential-handling surfaces have no corresponding threat model, so the artifact misleads a reader about where trust boundaries actually sit.

evidence.snippet: warning states the document predates the 0.1.0 REPL split; In-Scope C1-C17 and threats T1-T10 all describe the retired REPL surface, not the deploy CLI

recommended_actions: Regenerate `THREAT_MODEL.md` for the actual shipped surface (`deepagents_cli.deploy` bundler, MCP resolver, `config`/`model_config` credential handling), or clearly scope it down and remove the stale REPL sections.

findings.summary: The documented `mcp-servers add` workflow places an API key in a command-line argument, where it is visible to co-resident processes and shell history.
findings.description: The README usage block and the post-`init` welcome both instruct `--header X-Api-Key=$LANGSMITH_API_KEY`, so the secret is expanded onto the process command line — readable via `ps`/`/proc/<pid>/cmdline` by same-user and root processes and captured in shell history. The CLI itself handles the value correctly (never logging or printing it, redacting it to `***` on `mcp-servers get`), so this is a workflow/documentation hygiene issue rather than a CLI defect; the threat model assumes a single-user local machine, which bounds the exposure.

evidence.snippet: post-init welcome prints "--header X-Api-Key=$LANGSMITH_API_KEY" as the recommended auth option; README usage repeats it
usage example registers an MCP server with "--header X-Api-Key=$LANGSMITH_API_KEY" on the command line

recommended_actions: Prefer an env-var reference or stdin/prompt for header secrets, or document the argv-exposure caveat, so keys are not passed as visible command-line arguments.

findings.summary: README and DEVELOPMENT.md advertise a `deepagents dev` subcommand that is not wired into the CLI, so documented instructions fail.
findings.description: `README.md` and `DEVELOPMENT.md` both list the surface as `init, dev, deploy`, and `DEVELOPMENT.md` gives a concrete `deepagents_cli dev --config ...` example, but `main._dispatch_command` wires only `init`, `deploy`, `agents`, and `mcp-servers` — a `dev` invocation falls through to the REPL-redirect message and exits non-zero. This is a documentation-vs-implementation drift (user confusion), not a security control gap; confirm whether `dev` was removed or relocated and update the docs accordingly.

evidence.snippet: "this package contains only the deployment subcommands (init, dev, deploy)" — but no dev command is wired
_dispatch_command handles init/deploy/agents/mcp-servers only; any other command (incl. dev) hits _REPL_REDIRECT_MESSAGE and exit 1

recommended_actions: Remove the `dev` references from `README.md` and `DEVELOPMENT.md`, or wire the command, so the documented tool inventory matches the shipped surface.

positives.title: HTTPS-only transport with userinfo and proxy-env hardening
positives.description: `api_client._normalize_endpoint` forces the scheme to HTTPS and rejects any endpoint carrying userinfo, and the `httpx.Client` is built with `trust_env=False` so ambient proxy/TLS environment cannot redirect authenticated traffic; `config.py` additionally blocks project `.env` from setting endpoint/proxy/TLS keys.

positives.title: Symlink and path-escape rejection during bundle assembly
positives.description: Every project file read passes through `_ensure_project_contained`/`_read_project_text`, which reject symlinks and any path that resolves outside the project root, upholding the core "bundle only declared sources" guarantee.

positives.title: Confirmation gates on remote-mutating and destructive actions
positives.description: Deploying to an `agent_id` declared in `agent.json` requires an interactive y/N confirmation (`_confirm_agent_json_target`), and agent/MCP-server deletions and `init` overwrites are likewise gated behind confirmation or an explicit `--force`/`--yes`.

positives.title: MCP auth-header redaction on read
positives.description: `mcp-servers get` runs the server record through `_redact_mcp_server`/`_redact_mcp_header`, replacing every header `value` with `***` so auth headers are never printed to the terminal.

positives.title: Repo-local state ignored for authenticated requests
positives.description: `ApiClient.from_env` resolves auth and endpoint only from the environment and deliberately ignores repository-local deploy state, so a cloned, attacker-controlled project cannot silently steer where credentials are sent.

positives.title: Committed dependency lockfile with Dependabot coverage
positives.description: A pinned `uv.lock` is committed for `libs/cli` and `.github/dependabot.yml` schedules monthly `uv` and GitHub-Actions updates, giving reproducible installs and tracked upgrades.

positives.title: Current adversarial test coverage of the deploy surface
positives.description: The unit suite exercises attack scenarios directly — symlink/path-escape rejection, non-HTTPS and userinfo rejection, proxy-env isolation, delete confirmation, and header redaction — evidencing security testing of the shipped code.

log_files.no_logs_note: The CLI configures no logging handlers (stdlib `logging` diagnostics reach only stderr via the last-resort handler) and writes no action/audit log; the deploy-state JSON under `~/.deepagents/deployments/` records last-deploy metadata but is overwritten each run and is not an append-only trail — this absence is reflected in the Monitor Continuously score, not filed as a separate finding.

raise_posture.weighted_rationale: Established. Across the framework the tool has real, code-level controls on the categories that matter most for a bundling-and-deploy utility — domain is tightly scoped (four subcommands, no model client, containment-checked file reads), data boundaries are disciplined (only declared sources enter the bundle; project `.env` cannot steer endpoint/proxy/TLS; repo-local state is ignored for auth), and zero-trust transport and approval controls are present and tested. It is held back by a specific transport gap (MCP-URL TLS unenforced), mixed dependency-pinning, a stale threat model, and the near-absence of any durable action/audit record for the remote mutations it performs — the CLI prints results and keeps last-deploy state but logs no append-only trail of deploys, updates, or deletes.

categories.name: Limit Your Domain
categories.rationale: The shipped surface is exactly four deploy subcommands with no model client, no REPL, and no exec; bare invocations redirect and exit, `project.py` containment-checks every file read to the project root, and legacy `deepagents.toml`/`mcp.json` are rejected — domain is enforced in code, not just documented.

categories.name: Balance Your Knowledge Base
categories.rationale: The bundle is a pure function over the project's declared sources (`payload.py`), project `.env` is blocked from overriding endpoint/proxy/TLS (`config._PROJECT_DOTENV_BLOCKED_ENV_KEYS`), repo-local deploy state is intentionally ignored for auth, and `.env`/secret material is never folded into the payload.

categories.name: Implement Zero Trust
categories.rationale: Strong verified controls — HTTPS enforced with userinfo rejected, `trust_env=False`, confirmation gates on deploy-target/delete/overwrite, and symlink/path-escape rejection — are offset by the MCP-URL TLS gap (`mcp_resolver`/`commands` never check the scheme) and a documented workflow that puts credentials in argv.

categories.name: Manage Your Supply Chain
categories.rationale: A pinned `uv.lock` is committed and Dependabot tracks `libs/cli`, and most MIT dependencies carry upper bounds; the gap is that `deepagents` and `langsmith` are floor-pinned with no ceiling, so a PyPI `uv tool install` can resolve an unvetted major version.

categories.name: Build an AI Red Team
categories.rationale: The deploy surface has current adversarial tests (symlink/path-escape rejection, non-HTTPS and userinfo rejection, proxy-env isolation, delete confirmation, header redaction) and the code carries attack-motivated defenses, but the shipped `THREAT_MODEL.md` predates the REPL split and documents surfaces the package no longer contains.

categories.name: Monitor Continuously
categories.rationale: The CLI emits `print` results and keeps a last-write-wins deploy-state JSON under `~/.deepagents/deployments/`, but configures no logging handlers (diagnostics reach only stderr) and keeps no append-only audit trail of the remote agent/MCP deploys, updates, and deletes it performs.
